title: Laser-Assisted Patterning of Metallized Fabrics for Washable and Durable Electronic Textiles
abstract: Wearable electronic textiles (e-textiles) are increasingly being explored for continuous, noninvasive physiological monitoring; however, scalable fabrication of high-resolution circuitry with long-term mechanical and washing durability remains a major challenge. Conventional approaches, including screen printing, inkjet printing, and conductive-thread embroidery, enable the integration of conductive traces into garments but often suffer from limited patterning resolution, binder-related degradation, mechanical instability, and unreliable interfacing with electronic components. Here, we present a selective laser-assisted ablation method for directly defining conductive circuit traces on single-sided metallized fabrics (MFs) composed of woven, multi-stranded silver fiber yarns. This mask-free and chemical-free process enables rapid, digitally programmable patterning while preserving the structural integrity, flexibility, and breathability of the underlying textile. Importantly, localized laser heating simultaneously removes conductive fibers in selected regions and thermally fuses the exposed ends of adjacent silver yarns, thereby suppressing fraying and enhancing the mechanical robustness of the patterned circuit edges. Using a neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) laser tuned for high absorption by silver, controlled ablation at energy densities of 8–26.5 J·cm −2 produced well-defined insulating regions without compromising the conductivity of neighboring traces. Surface and elemental analyses confirmed nearly complete silver removal, with residual silver content below 3% in the ablated areas. The resulting laser-ablated metallized fabric (LA-MF) exhibited low sheet resistance (approximately 2 mΩ/sq.), retained more than 94% of its initial conductivity after 10000 bending cycles, and maintained stable electrical performance after more than 20 machine-washing cycles. As a proof of concept, a 16-electrode electrical impedance tomography (EIT) array was patterned directly onto the MF and integrated into a compression garment for noninvasive lung-function monitoring. The textile electrodes enabled real-time impedance imaging, and an embedded convolutional neural network accurately classified respiratory states, including normal breathing and breath-hold conditions, even after repeated laundering. This laser-assisted patterning framework provides a robust, scalable, and manufacturing-compatible route for integrating high-performance circuit architectures directly into fabrics for wearable sensing, healthcare monitoring, and next-generation smart textile applications.

title: Electrospinning Technology and Electrospun Materials from Past to Present
abstract: Electrospinning has evolved from a foundational scientific phenomenon into a versatile and transformative platform technology for fabricating nanofibers. Despite its long history, recent developments in the area have been rapid. The technique enables effective regulation of fiber diameter, composition, and architecture, presenting a broad prospect in advanced research and industrial applications. This review provides a holistic examination of the advancements in electrospinning technology and electrospun materials, focusing on the evolution of the technology itself from lab-scale to industrial-scale systems, as well as the material structural designs and industrial applications. The single-needle—multi-needle—needleless evolution of the technology forms the mainstream development trend for electrospinning technology, decorated by niche and significant innovations for specific applications. These systems are all based on the same fundamentals of electrospinning, which is the starting point of this review. The discussion extends to the structural design of electrospun materials across multi-dimensional scales, ranging from one-dimensional nanofibers, two-dimensional membranes, to three-dimensional bulk materials. These hierarchical structures underpin the groundbreaking multifunctionality of electrospun nanomaterials, enabling their successful deployment in filtration and separation, thermal and moisture management textiles, energy storage and harvesting devices, aerospace, and biomedical and sensing applications. Finally, we highlight prevailing challenges and future perspectives aimed at expanding application frontiers, enhancing mechanical durability, achieving sustainable and scalable manufacturing, and integrating with smart systems. This review is expected to serve as a comprehensive reference on the advancement of electrospinning technology to date.

title: Hybrid Metal–ceramic Fiber Frameworks Based on Designs of Metallic Coatings for High-temperature Resistant Temperature–pressure Sensing
abstract: Extreme thermal environments demand sensors with two mutually exclusive properties: flexibility (to conform curved surfaces and withstand dynamic stress) and high-temperature tolerance (to avoid degradation above 400 °C). However, existing polymer-based flexible sensors are thermally unstable, and conventional high-temperature sensors of ceramic and metal are inflexible. Herein, we address this challenge with a hybrid metal–ceramic framework of Pt x Au 1−x coated ZrO 2 -Al 2 O 3 nanofibers (Pt x Au 1−x @ZANF), enabling flexible dual-functional temperature–pressure sensing up to 800 °C. Systematic studies on solid-state dewetting, nano-grain melting, and phase stability identified Au-rich Pt 0.15 Au 0.85 as optimal: it retains a single face-centered cubic phase and low resistivity (< 1 order of magnitude increase) after 2 h at 800 °C in air, outperforming pure Pt/Au and Pt-rich alloys (prone to phase separation/spheroidization). Laser-patterned electrodes on Pt 0.15 Au 0.85 @ZANF yield a dual-functional temperature–pressure sensor, which exhibits both high-temperature resistance and flexibility. The sensor exhibited a sensitivity range of 0.019 kPa −1 to 0.054 kPa −1 and demonstrated stability over 360 cycles (≥ 3 h) at 800 °C, far exceeding the maximum operating temperature of other reported temperature–pressure sensors (≤ 300 °C). This framework combines flexibility and high-temperature tolerance, two essential properties for reliable sensing on curved industrial robot joints, chemical plant reactors, and spacecraft surfaces. Graphical Abstract

title: Structure-Guided Design of Lignocellulosic Fibers: From Biomass Architecture to Functional Materials
abstract: Although lignocellulosic fibers offer a promising route to low-carbon functional materials, current research remains fragmented across feedstock selection, pretreatment, fiber formation, and application-specific optimization, which limits the establishment of predictive structure–process–performance relationships. To address this problem, this review proposes a structure-guided framework that connects native lignocellulosic architecture, controlled deconstruction, fiber assembly, interfacial engineering, and sustainability-oriented applications. Lignocellulosic biomass is examined as a structurally programmable feedstock in which cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and lignin–carbohydrate interfaces jointly define processing constraints and design opportunities. We analyze how pretreatment, nanofiber generation, dissolution–regeneration, spinning, self-assembly, and post-treatment regulate key structural descriptors, including cellulose chain integrity, crystallinity, orientation, pore topology, surface chemistry, lignin state, lignin–carbohydrate complex (LCC) retention, and interfacial bonding. On this basis, we show that application diversity in textiles, packaging, separation, energy devices, electronics, and biomedicine arises not from isolated material categories, but from the repeated reorganization of common structural descriptors to meet different functional priorities. Route-specific sustainability hotspots and application- and performance-based life-cycle assessment are further discussed. We conclude that the future development of lignocellulosic fibers requires a shift from empirical optimization toward predictive, scalable, and sustainability-guided design. Graphical Abstract

title: Passive Chips-in-Yarn Integration for On-Fabric Batteryless Identification and Sensing
abstract: Smart clothing has the potential to monitor the body continuously, but most current systems still rely on rigid electronic modules, batteries, and wired connections. These components reduce flexibility, comfort, washability, and long-term usability. Here, we report a passive chips-in-yarn strategy for creating battery-free electronic yarns that can be integrated directly into fabrics. In this approach, radio frequency identification (RFID) chips are embedded inside yarn structures, allowing the yarns to be wirelessly powered and read by an external RFID reader without onboard batteries. The RFID chip is connected to conductive filaments that act as yarn-shaped antennas, while local encapsulation and a braided sheath protect the chip–filament junction during textile manufacturing and use. By engineering different antenna geometries, RFID yarns enable multiple functions: ID-only yarns for garment life-cycle identification, deformation-sensitive yarns for passive movement monitoring through wireless signal changes, and temperature-sensing yarns for distributed on-body thermal mapping. The resulting RFID yarns showed mechanical robustness, wash durability, and compatibility with textile weaving integration. With multiple chip-enabled yarns embedded into garments, this work demonstrates a fabric-scale sensing network that is lightweight, battery-free, and maintenance-free. This work advances smart textiles from module-attached wearable devices toward textile-native sensing systems, where passive electronic functions are embedded directly within the yarn structure. Graphical Abstract

title: Bifunctional Fluorinated Iron-MOF Incorporated PVDF-HFP Nanofibrous Mat-Based High-Performance Triboelectric Nanogenerators for Self-Powered Biomotion and Respiration Monitoring
abstract: The triboelectric performance of ferroelectric fluoropolymers is intrinsically governed by interfacial polarization and electroactive β-phase, which collectively enhance dielectric properties, charge retention ability, and surface charge density. Herein, this work reports the first development of a bifunctional nanofibrous mat by incorporating fluorinated iron-metal-organic framework (Iron-MOF) into poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP) nanofibers, simultaneously promoting electroactive β-phase and charge retention through a facile one-step self-assembly electrospinning strategy, enabling a high-performance wearable triboelectric nanogenerator. Fluorinated Iron-MOF functions as an efficient nucleating and charge-modulating agent, inducing strong hydrogen bonding and interfacial polarization between MOF-polymer (–CF 2 –CH 2 –) dipoles. This synergistic strategy promotes uniaxial nanocrystal alignment, achieves a significantly improved β-phase fraction of 97.48%, and enhances the dielectric constant by 205.88%. Owing to its bifunctionalities, the surface potential and charge-retention efficiency of composite nanofibers increased 2.5- and 9.5-fold, respectively. Leveraging these advancements, a bifunctional nanofibrous-based triboelectric nanogenerator (BNFs-TENG) delivered outstanding electrical output (684 V, 26.2 μA, and 2.1 W m −2 ), outperforming state-of-the-art MOF-based TENGs. Furthermore, BNFs-TENG served as a self-powered wearable smart band, delivering remarkable pressure sensitivity (5.41 V kPa −1 , 0.25–5 kPa), enabling intelligent respiratory rehabilitation progress, and real-time monitoring of respiratory behaviour and physical activity. This work establishes a versatile fluorinated MOF-fluoropolymer interfacial engineering strategy that achieves superior device performance and next-generation self-powered wearable healthcare technologies. Graphical Abstract

title: Recyclable Thermoplastic Structural Electrolytes Enabling Customized High-Strength Structural Batteries
abstract: Structural batteries capable of simultaneously bearing load and storing electrochemical energy represent a transformative paradigm for next-generation electric vehicles and aerospace systems. However, the intrinsically poor ion transport of conventional epoxy-based structural electrolytes hinders the practical implementation of structural batteries. Herein, a sustainable composite solid structural electrolyte is innovatively developed by employing polyethylene oxide as a highly ion-conductive matrix and cellulose acetate as a mechanically reinforcing phase. This uniquely synergistic design delivers a high ionic conductivity of 0.33 mS cm −1 and a high tensile strength of 8.79 MPa, effectively reconciling electrochemical and mechanical functionalities. The thermoplastic structural electrolyte is directly integrated with the carbon fiber (CF)-based electrodes via standard compression molding to fabricate the resulting structural batteries, demonstrating a higher tensile strength of 371.36 MPa with an energy density of 13.69 Wh kg −1 , which surpasses that of the conventional CF-reinforced structural batteries. Notably, the cellulose-based thermoplastic architecture enables exceptional recyclability and processability, allowing secondary assembly into customized complex structural automobile/aerospace components without compromising energy storage performance. This forward-looking work presents a novel, viable strategy for designing recyclable structural solid electrolytes compatible with industrial compression molding process, offering a sustainable and scalable pathway for CF-based structural energy storage large-scale applications. Graphical Abstract

title: Multifunctional Magnetic Soft Fibers: A Platform for Wearable, Biomedical, and Soft Robotic Systems
abstract: Magnetic soft fibers (MSFs) have emerged as a promising class of stimuli-responsive materials that combine magnetic functionality, mechanical compliance, programmable magnetization, and multifunctional performance within fiber-based architectures. Their ability to enable wireless actuation, adaptive deformation, sensing, and electrical energy generation has attracted growing interest in wearable electronics, biomedical devices, and soft robotic systems. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the fundamental principles, material systems, fabrication methods, magnetization strategies, and emerging applications of MSFs. The review highlights that recent advances in material design, scalable fabrication technologies, and programmable magnetization have enabled MSFs to evolve from simple magnetic composites into multifunctional platforms capable of actuation, sensing, and energy harvesting within a single fiber system. Furthermore, the integration of electrical, optical, and fluidic functionalities has expanded their potential in wearable monitoring, minimally invasive biomedical devices, adaptive soft actuators, and remotely actuated robotic systems. Key challenges associated with material optimization, scalable manufacturing, and long-term reliability are also identified, along with emerging opportunities in intelligent design and adaptive control. By consolidating recent progress, identifying critical challenges, and outlining future research directions, this review provides a roadmap for the development of next-generation multifunctional magnetic soft-fiber technologies.

title: Skin-Inspired Controllable Microcrack Electronic Skin with High Signal-to-Noise Ratio for High-Fidelity Pulse Wave Monitoring
abstract: Wearable electronic skin (E-skin) with high sensitivity and stable response characteristics holds significant promise for human body monitoring. To address the critical bottleneck of stochastic microcrack morphology and poor structural controllability inherent in conventional MXene-based microcrack sensors, we present a skin-inspired, hierarchically structured E-skin in which ordered regulation of MXene microcracks is achieved through a pre-stretching–spray-coating coupling strategy. Benefiting from the synergistic interplay between structural engineering and conductive pathway modulation, the device achieves a sensitivity of 6.17 kPa –1 over a pressure range of 0–60 kPa, along with a cycling stability exceeding 12000 loading–unloading cycles, a rapid response time of 40 ms, and a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 30.64 dB. By combining discrete wavelet transform (DWT) and continuous wavelet transform (CWT) for multi-scale analysis of radial and carotid arterial pulse signals, a dominant frequency of approximately 1.3 Hz (78 bpm) was extracted, validating the device’s high-resolution capability for detecting subtle physiological signals. This MXene-based microcrack E-skin offers a novel technical approach for the controllable fabrication of microcracks and demonstrates considerable potential for applications in wearable medical monitoring. Graphical Abstract

title: Continuous Spinning of Tough, Robust, Ionic-Conductive, and Stable Fibers for Reliable Signal Transmission
abstract: Fiber-shaped ionic conductors are ideal for bioelectronic interfaces due to their structural and functional similarities to biological tissues. However, achieving high mechanical strength, superior conductivity, and long-term environmental stability within a scalable fiber format remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report a design strategy to fabricate tough, robust, ionic-conductive and stable (TRIS) fibers via continuous UV-assisted spinning of a quaternary deep eutectic solvent. The core lies in the synergistic interplay between a highly dynamic hydrogen-bonding supramolecular network and dynamic carboxyl–zirconium coordination complexes. This molecular architecture enables TRIS fibers to simultaneously realize a high Young’s modulus (approximately 8.7 MPa) and excellent ionic conductivity (approximately 0.896 S/m). Furthermore, the fibers exhibit exceptional environmental stability, maintaining stable performance for over 1 year in ambient conditions. As a demonstration, TRIS fibers function as ionic cables that can transmit high-fidelity signals under strain (approximately 50%) and, notably, as artificial nerves to bridge a severed sciatic nerve in rats. The successful restoration of sensory and motor functions in vivo highlights the potential of TRIS fibers as functional neural replacements. This work provides a scalable and robust platform for the development of next-generation, tissue-like implantable bioelectronics.

title: Ultrasoft Core–Shell Inorganic Nanoyarns for Energy and Sensing Applications
abstract: Inorganic nanoyarns with high electrical conductivity, tunable redox activity, and outstanding chemical/thermal stability are promising components for high-performance multifunctional fibers. However, integrating inorganic functionality with the softness, durability, and processability required for wearable fiber systems remains a major challenge. Here we present ultrasoft core–shell nanoyarns composed of inorganic nanoribbon cores and polymer shells with exceptional mechanical compliance while maintaining high electrical and chemical performance. The inorganic core provides multifunctionality and structural diversity with single-layer, particle-decorated, and multilayer sandwich architectures. A grounded-core electrospinning strategy is introduced to form porous polymer shells around the inorganic cores, providing mechanical reinforcement, electrical insulation, and diffusion pathways for reactive species within a resilient, flexible framework. The proposed core–shell nanoyarns function as efficient water-splitting electrodes, deliver a high volumetric energy density in fiber-type supercapacitors, and operate as force sensors capable of detecting forces at the tens-of-micronewton level. These results establish the core–shell nanoyarn as a universal and scalable platform for wearable energy and sensing systems. Graphical Abstract

title: Correction: Self-Powered Bifunctional Fiber Devices Integrating Alternating Current Electroluminescence and Stable Zinc-Ion Batteries
Engineering Electrospun Nanofibers for Intelligent Wearables
abstract: Abstract The rapid development of intelligent wearables poses significant challenges for textile materials requiring high strength, toughness, good formability, and multifunctionality. Electrospinning generates nanofibers of high flexibility, breathability, and specific surface area. High-performance fibrous material is suitable for next-generation wearables. This review examines and summarizes electrospinning and the morphology of nanofibers, as well as the methods for modification. Moreover, the application of integrated nanofiber-based intelligent wearable systems in many areas is discussed. Powered by engineering electrospun nanofibers, intelligent wearables have been used in fields such as health monitoring, intelligent biotherapy, and next-generation intelligent textiles. Wearable monitoring devices can continuously monitor the health status of the human body in real time. Intelligent medical systems can use the monitoring information to achieve targeted drug delivery, reducing dependence on medical devices. Hiding these intelligent devices within textiles is the ultimate goal of wearable devices. Such fabrics combine functionality and comfort, providing a solution for the next-generation intelligent textiles. Finally, current challenges in the field are discussed, and future work is proposed. In short, electrospun nanofiber material can lead wearable technology toward increased integration and intelligence with promising solutions for future healthcare and textile applications. Graphical abstract

title: Bioadaptive Acoustoelectric Fibers for Wireless Neuromodulation of Central Sensitization in Chronic Migraine
abstract: Chronic migraine, a neurological disorder often refractory to conventional medication, necessitates novel therapeutic strategies. Here, bioadaptive acoustoelectric fibers (BAEFs) are developed for ultrasound-driven vagus nerve stimulation, exhibiting high stretchability (830%) and a low Young’s modulus (0.718 MPa). Owing to their biofluidic permeability and hydrogen-bonding capability, the BAEFs promote interfacial fluid migration and enhance adhesion, enabling them to self-wrap securely around nerve surfaces and maintain stable attachment for at least 21 days. The BAEFs incorporate high-performance piezoelectric particles synthesized by nanoconfinement self-assembly of phenylalanine dipeptide within a zirconium aminobenzenedicarboxylate metal–organic framework. Functioning as a sensitive ultrasound receiver, the BAEFs leverage the octahedral structure of particles to generate multi-orientation piezoelectric responses, effectively activating neural responses under ultrasound incidence at 60°. In a chronic migraine model, ultrasound-triggered vagus nerve stimulation via the BAEFs inhibited overactivation of neurons, downregulated Fos proto-oncogene, AP-1 transcription factor subunit and calcitonin gene-related peptide, and alleviated comorbid anxiety and depressive behaviors, leading to significant migraine relief. This work establishes ultrasound-induced bioelectronic modulation via BAEFs as a promising, clinically translatable therapy for chronic migraine. Graphical Abstract

title: Reinforced Poly(Ionic Liquid)-in-Salt Electrolytes for Highly Stable Solid-State Lithium Metal Batteries
abstract: Solid-state polymer electrolytes (SPEs) are promising for high-safety, high-energy-density lithium metal batteries, but their adoption is limited by low room-temperature ionic conductivity and insufficient mechanical robustness. This study reports an improved SPE architecture consisting of a three-dimensional (3D) polyacrylonitrile (PAN)–Li 6.4 La 3 Zr 1.4 Ta 0.6 O 12 (LLZTO) fibrous skeleton infused with a polymer electrolyte ionic liquid (PIL), which promotes lithium-salt dissociation, accelerates Li + transport, and enhances mechanical strength. The resulting SPE achieves an ionic conductivity of up to 0.51 mS cm −1 . Li|Li symmetric cells using a 40-µm-thick SPE cycle stably for 2500 h at 0.2 mA cm −2 with a low overpotential of 30 mV. In Li|LiFePO 4 (LFP) full cells, the electrolyte enables 86.8% capacity retention after 1000 cycles at 0.5 C and maintains stable operation at 130 °C. Flexible pouch-cell tests further confirm improved safety and durability under harsh conditions, highlighting the potential of this SPE design for high-voltage lithium metal batteries.

title: Enzymatic Processes of Fiber Assemblies: Property Enhancement, Functionalization, and Reutilization
abstract: Enzyme technology has emerged as a pivotal strategy in the processes of varied fiber assemblies such as yarns, woven and knitted fabrics, and apparel, complementing conventional physical and chemical approaches. This review summarizes the types and application strategies of enzymes commonly employed in fiber processing. From the perspective of fiber-specific properties, we elaborate on how hydrolase-based treatments (e.g., amylases, pectinases, cellulases, and proteases) maximize the inherent characteristics of fibers by precisely modulating their microstructure, surface wettability, and mechanical properties. Furthermore, we highlight recent advances in fiber functionalization mediated by oxidoreductases (e.g., laccase and horseradish peroxidase (HRP)) and transferases (e.g., transglutaminase (TGase)). These strategies harness fiber structures and enzymatic pathways for diverse textile functionalities, including laccase-mediated cellulose aldolization, HRP-catalyzed wool thiol-ene chemistry, and TGase-induced protein cross-linking, etc. Representative applications are categorized into three domains: comfort, healthcare, and protective textiles. In addition, the recycling of waste textiles has also been mentioned, focusing on the challenges of enzymatic hydrolysis of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) fibers. Finally, we critically assess the advantages and key challenges of enzymatic catalysis over conventional fiber processing technologies, including limited enzyme accessibility, the trade-off between substrate specificity and structural complexity, insufficient enhancement of fiber performance and functionality, and high production costs. Looking forward, we outline two complementary future directions for enzymatic catalysis in fiber processing: artificial intelligence (AI)-guided enzyme design and novel catalytic technologies for fiber processing, aiming to integrate biocatalysis more deeply with fiber manufacturing. Graphical abstract

title: Liquid-Metal-Enabled, Bifunctional Core-Sheath Metafibers for Sensitive Biomotion Sensing and Radiative Personal Thermal Management
abstract: Combining radiative cooling with electronic sensing is crucial for the next generation of adaptive wearables. However, it remains challenging to achieve both efficient optical–thermal regulation and highly sensitive biomotion-sensing fiber architectures. Here, we develop porous core-sheath fibers that utilize the dual effects of liquid metal (LM) to integrate motion sensing and passive radiative cooling functions in a single fiber. The encapsulated LM microdroplets within the polymer act as both reconfigurable conductive networks and optical–thermal modulation units. These fibers exhibit excellent mechanical robustness, with an elongation at break exceeding 1000%. Owing to the piezoresistive LM network, the fibers exhibit sensing performance, featuring a strain detection limit of 0.01%, a response time of 62 ms, and a durability over 20000 cycles. Meanwhile, LM microdroplets serve dual roles as microscale reflectors and efficient heat transfer media. The synergistic effect between the porous polymer and LM microdroplets endows the fabrics with excellent radiative cooling capabilities, achieving a solar reflectance of 95.3% and a mid-infrared emissivity of 96.1%. Outdoor tests show the sustained subambient cooling of 5.2–6.3 °C and annual energy saving of 80–320 MJ/m 2 year −1 . Furthermore, these fibers enable simultaneous real-time gesture recognition and personal thermal management, thereby providing a versatile platform for multifunctional smart textiles.

title: From Traditional Depolymerization to Value-Added Upgrading: Upcycling of PET Fibers with Sustainable Chemistry and Renewable Energy
abstract: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is not only a major packaging plastic but also the dominant polyester used in fibers and textiles, including apparel, carpets, nonwovens, filtration media, and industrial fabrics. The growing accumulation of post-consumer PET bottles and textiles poses severe challenges to conventional recycling and accelerates the release of fibrous microplastics. Upcycling PET fibers into value-added chemicals, fuels, and functional materials therefore offers an important route toward sustainable fiber circularity. This work focuses on the mechanistic underpinnings of sustainable chemical strategies and the successful integration of renewable energy sources for converting PET into high-value chemicals. We first outline the fundamental cleavage chemistry of the PET ester bond. Subsequently, exciting progress in thermocatalysis, electrocatalysis, and photocatalysis is critically examined in detail, combining the PET waste transformation with sustainable chemistry and renewable energy. Next, the existing challenges and future perspectives are featured, aiming to advance molecular-level understanding and guide the design of closed-loop circular chemical processes. We envision a sustainable future where discarded plastics and fibers evolve from being an ecological concern to becoming a valuable chemical resource within the circular economy. Graphical Abstract

title: Electrical Fibers for Intelligent Textiles: From Conductivity–Flexibility Trade-offs to Scalable Systems
abstract: Intelligent textiles capable of sensing, communication, and energy interaction require electrical fibers (elecfibers, ECFs) to function as system-level building units rather than passive conductors. Beyond charge transport, ECFs must integrate electrical performance with mechanical compliance, interfacial stability, and device functionality within deformable textile architectures. This transition is constrained by four coupled challenges: balancing conductivity and flexibility; managing degradation from multifunctional interfaces; bridging the gap between fiber-level properties and textile-scale behavior governed by contact resistance and dynamic deformation; and translating laboratory performance into scalable manufacturing and long-term reliability under washing, sweating, abrasion, and environmental exposure. This review addresses these challenges through a cross-scale, problem-oriented framework. We examine conduction mechanisms and fiber architectures that govern the conductivity–flexibility trade-off, followed by multifunctional integration in thermal, electromagnetic, sensing, communication, and energy systems, with an emphasis on interfacial reliability. Cross-scale electrical behavior is analyzed from local pathways to textile networks and system-level performance, while scalable fabrication and reliability evaluation are identified as prerequisites for deployment. By redefining ECFs as system-level components, this review establishes design principles centered on conductive continuity, interfacial stability, and cross-scale integration, enabling intelligent textiles with reliable, durable, and manufacturable performance. Graphical Abstract

title: Energy‑Tiered Functional Materials for Personal Thermal‑Moisture Management
abstract: Personal thermal-moisture management (PTMM) provides a targeted approach to improving human comfort while reducing building energy consumption. However, its practical application remains limited by two major barriers. The theory-reality gap arises from the limited ability of current models to describe multiphysics coupling within dynamic human–clothing–environment systems. The materials-system gap reflects the difficulty of translating strong laboratory performance into wearable and durable functional garments. This review proposes a new three-tier classification framework based on energy use, including zero-energy passive systems, low-energy intelligent switching systems, and high-energy active driving systems. Using this framework, we summarize recent advances in smart textiles for PTMM and discuss their thermal-moisture performance, energy consumption, durability, practical limitations, and possible solutions. This review aims to address the main barriers in the field and support the translation of dynamic thermal-moisture management garments from laboratory research to everyday use. Graphical abstract

title: Advanced Zero-Energy Radiative Cooling Fibrous Fabrics for Sustainable Personal Thermal Management
abstract: Passive daytime radiative cooling fibrous fabrics (RCFFs) represent a potential zero-energy solution for personal thermal management, addressing the dual challenges of escalating global warming/extreme heat events and the massive energy footprint of traditional space cooling systems. While RCFFs have garnered tremendous research attention, existing reviews mainly focus on material design and optical modulation, lacking systematic elaboration of their unique structure–property relationships, heat transfer mechanisms, multifunctional integration, and industrial translation. This review provides a comprehensive overview of RCFFs. We first elucidate the fundamental heat transfer principles and standardized performance evaluation metrics of RCFFs, followed by a systematic summary of spectral design strategies and structural engineering from single fibers to fabrics. Then, we highlight the advances in multimodal synergistic thermal management and versatile functional integration, including colored fabrics, dynamic thermoregulation, flexible electronics, energy harvesting, and wound healing dressings. Finally, we discuss existing challenges hindering practical application and provide future developments on next-generation intelligent RCFFs, offering systematic guidance for the design and commercialization of high-performance personal thermal management fabrics. Graphical Abstract

title: Fibrous Network-Based Interlocking Interfaces for Aqueous-Stable and Mechanically Robust Bioelectronics
abstract: Bioelectronics interface with living systems to capture physiological signals and advance our understanding of health. However, the aqueous and dynamically deforming nature of biological tissues poses significant challenges to the structural stability and long-term reliability of bioelectronic devices, particularly at internal interfaces between dissimilar materials. Here, we report robust and stretchable bioelectronics (RSB) that achieve exceptional aqueous and mechanical stability by introducing a mechanically interlocking interface inspired by traditional wooden mortise–tenon structures. In the RSB, conductive poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS) is integrated with fibrous network-decorated elastomeric matrices via spin coating and laser-induced phase separation. As a result, the bioelectronics maintain conductivity under tensile strains exceeding 100% and stable impedance after continuous immersion in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for over 30 days. Moreover, the RSB enables high-fidelity electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring and electrical stimulation-mediated restoration of normal sinus rhythm in rat models. Beyond biological systems, the bioelectronics can be integrated onto robotic fingertips, establishing a paradigm for robot-assisted acquisition of physiological signals through direct human–robot contact. The flexible interlocking interface provides a versatile platform for robust, stretchable, and long-lasting bioelectronic systems across biological and robotic interfaces. Graphical abstract

title: Silk Fibroin-Based Flexible Electronics: A Mesoscopic Pathway Toward Human–Machine Interconnection
abstract: Silk fibroin, a natural textile material spun by silkworms over millennia, is emerging as a transformative platform for integrating human intelligence with artificial intelligence. Its core innovation lies in the meso-functionalization strategy, which precisely programs protein refolding and hierarchical assembly. This strategy groundbreakingly resolves the long-standing performance paradox among biocompatibility, mechanical compliance, and high-fidelity signal acquisition in bioelectronic interfaces, thereby providing a solution that is difficult to achieve with other material systems. This transformation elevates the traditional fiber into a programmable electronic material, capable not only of conformal and seamless skin contact but also of constructing dynamic conductive networks, and even pioneering the fabrication of neuromorphic memristors that emulate synaptic plasticity. Furthermore, silk fibroin systems, reshaped through meso-engineering, are poised to catalyze a novel paradigm for deep integration between biological systems and artificial intelligence. When coupled with AI-driven intelligent analytics and closed-loop feedback control, the system can decode human physiological states in real time into machine-interpretable command signals, while simultaneously delivering adaptive regulatory responses back to the body. This bidirectional interface breaks through the conventional boundaries of human–machine interaction, with application prospects spanning frontier domains such as wearable health monitoring, invasive brain–computer interfaces, and cognitive augmentation technologies. Ultimately, while honoring its heritage as a natural textile, silk fibroin opens a pathway toward deep biointegration that is both sustainable and exceptionally biocompatible. Along this pathway, ancient material wisdom collides with future artificial intelligence to spark synergistic innovation, ultimately empowering human intelligence to reach new heights through human–machine co-evolution.

title: Flexible Loofah Fiber and Face Mask-Based Triboelectric Nanogenerator for Motion Sensing and Smart Home Applications
abstract: The growing demand for sustainable energy harvesting technologies necessitates the development of eco-friendly and low-cost triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) derived from renewable and waste resources. Herein, we report on the fabrication of TENG by integrating a naturally derived loofah sponge fiber with recycled polypropylene (PP) obtained from discarded face mask, establishing a synergistic platform for both energy harvesting and sensing. The alkali-modified loofah sponge (MLS) fiber acts as an efficient positive triboelectric layer owing to its cellulose rich composition and hierarchically porous structure, which significantly enhances effective contact area, and improves triboelectric properties. The recycled mask-derived PP serves as a negative triboelectric layer, enabling efficient electron transfer and stable device operation. The resulting MLS-TENG delivers a voltage of 186.3 V, a current of 2.8 μA, and power density of 1.1 W/m 2 . Excellent mechanical durability is demonstrated with negligible performance degradation over 10000 contact-separation cycles. Furthermore, practical applicability of the MLS-TENG device is demonstrated through a smart home control system, where multiple TENG units are integrated with a microcontroller to achieve touch-controlled ON/OFF switching of household lighting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a smart home-oriented TENG system constructed entirely from waste-recyclable and natural materials, highlighting a scalable pathway for next-generation smart electronics. Graphical Abstract

title: Mechanically Decoupled Multimodal Tactile Perception Enabled by a Janus Textile Architecture
abstract: Tactile perception of surface properties is crucial for advanced robotics, yet conventional multimodal sensors suffer from mechanically coupled transduction that causes stress dissipation, signal interference, and complex decoupling. Here, we report a Janus-structured textile sensor that enables mechanically selective multimodal perception via physically decoupled force pathways. The Janus architecture integrates a conductive layer responsive to normal compression and a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)-coated dielectric layer sensitive to sliding, intrinsically separating piezoresistive and triboelectric signals without algorithmic decoupling. This structurally decoupled design effectively suppresses stress dissipation, enhances stress-transfer efficiency, and generates intrinsically distinguishable tactile signal fingerprints without relying on complex algorithmic decoupling. Benefiting from this mechanically selective transduction mechanism, the sensor exhibits excellent static and dynamic sensing capability, together with robust hydrophobicity, self-cleaning capability, and abrasion resistance. Assisted by machine learning-enabled feature analysis, the sensor achieves recognition accuracies of 99.6% for texture classification and 94.5% for material identification across 21 distinct samples. Furthermore, an integrated robotic tactile cognition system is constructed, enabling closed-loop tactile sensing especially the simultaneous surface texture and material recognition. This work establishes a mechanically selective tactile transduction strategy for physically separated multimodal perception, providing a scalable platform for next-generation robotic skins, embodied perception systems, and intelligent human–machine interfaces. Graphical abstract

title: Therapeutic Closure: Electro-mechanically Synergistic Sutures for Scarless Repair of High-Tension Wounds
abstract: High mechanical tension during wound closure typically triggers a pathological scarring cascade. Conventional surgical sutures act merely as passive tissue approximators, lacking the capacity to actively modulate this detrimental microenvironment. Herein, we establish a “closure as treatment” paradigm through the development of an electromechanically synergistic smart suture (S@VP@PPy) designed for scarless repair of high-tension wounds. The system features a hierarchical bilayer architecture comprising a verteporfin (VP)-loaded chitosan/gelatin drug reservoir and a conductive polypyrrole (PPy) outer coating. Transcriptomic and spatiotemporal protein analyses reveal a molecular division of labor. VP pharmacologically intercepts the transduction of mechanical stress into profibrotic cascades via YAP inhibition, concurrently resolving hyperinflammation and softening the extracellular matrix (ECM) by redirecting fibroblast fate. Within this softened permissive niche, PPy-mediated bioelectric stimulation accelerates re-epithelialization and activates the Wnt/β-catenin pathway to drive hair placode invagination. In a rat dorsal high-tension model, this spatiotemporal cooperation successfully intercepts the “tension-inflammation-fibrosis” cascade, culminating in scarless healing with de novo appendage regeneration. Graphical Abstract

title: Scalable Graphene Fiber-Mediated Aramid Papers via Hierarchical Topology Network Reconstruction for Highly Integrated Thermal Management and Microwave Absorption
abstract: Aramid-based materials integrating electromagnetic wave (EMW) absorption and thermal dissipation are in urgent demand to mitigate electromagnetic interference and heat accumulation in high-frequency and high-power-density electronics. However, achieving broadband synergistic enhancement at low filler loading remains a great challenge due to the trade-off between electromagnetic control and phonon transport in hierarchical fibrous networks. Herein, we propose a graphene fibers (GFs)-mediated modulation strategy to construct an aspect-ratio-tailored hierarchical percolation network within an aramid fiber paper (AFP) matrix via a scalable wet-papermaking process. By decoupling GF content and fiber length, the topological configuration and electromagnetic parameters of the hierarchical network are precisely tailored to bridge the gap between dielectric loss and thermal conduction. At a low loading of 4 wt.% GF, the optimized GF-modified AFP (GAFP) achieves a minimum reflection loss ( RL min ) of −82.6 dB and an effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of 2.4 GHz at a matching thickness of 2.55 mm, while delivering an exceptional in-plane thermal conductivity ( K ) of 4.1 W·m −1 ·K −1 . The resulting GAFP enables selective electromagnetic wave absorption covering the C, X, and Ku bands through network adjustments. Moreover, a mechanical compensation effect of high-aspect-ratio GFs mitigates the strength degradation typically associated with functional fillers. This work provides a universal network topology design framework for multifunctional fiber-reinforced composites in aerospace and advanced electronics. Graphical Abstract

title: Biomimetic Architected Ligaments with Programmable Non-linear Mechanical Behavior via Braiding
abstract: Natural ligaments achieve joint stability and mobility through hierarchical fibrous architectures encoding non-linear and deformation dependent mechanics, which remain elusive in artificial substitutes. Here, we report a bioinspired braiding strategy for artificial ligaments with programmable mechanical responses. By encoding knot structure, braiding length, and strand count, we achieve ligaments exhibiting tunable non-linear J-shaped force–displacement behavior with independently tunable deformation of the toe region and stiffness of the linear region. This programmability arises from hierarchical deformation, knot reconfiguration governing compliance onset, while structure-mediated strain transmission coordinates global deformation. Integrating mechanical characterization with machine learning enables mapping natural ligament mechanics onto an architected design space for data-driven configuration discovery. The resulting artificial ligaments reproduce non-linear mechanical responses with up to 99% similarity and enable biomimetic joint motions in mechanical validation. By establishing architecture as a programmable mechanical variable, this work provides a new paradigm for inverse design of artificial ligaments across biomedical and robotic applications.

title: Highly Transparent, Flexible, and Ultrathin Piezocomposite with Moth-Eye-Inspired Nanopatterns for Self-Cleaning and Water Droplet Energy-Harvesting
abstract: In this study, a piezoelectric nanogenerator (PENG) integrated with a moth-eye nanopatterned (MENP) perfluoropolyether (PFPE) film was fabricated using electrospinning, metal electroplating, spin-coating, and photolithography. The combination of these techniques enables the ultrathin MENP-PENG to possess high transparency, high sensitivity, and enhanced energy-harvesting performance, which are difficult to achieve simultaneously in conventional PENGs. Under an 11 mg water droplet impact, the MENP-PENG generated an output voltage of 1.0 V through a morphology-assisted hybrid response involving deformation-mediated piezoelectric transduction of the piezoelectric layer and liquid–solid contact electrification/electrostatic induction at the MENP/water interface, corresponding to a static-equivalent gravitational load of 100 μN. Owing to its self-cleaning and anti-reflective properties, the MENP-PENG shows potential as a transparent protective platform for electric vehicle camera modules. These results demonstrate that the materials design and fabrication strategy proposed here provide an effective route toward transparent, flexible, and high-performance PENGs for emerging electric vehicle camera applications. Graphical Abstract

title: Strain-Tolerant Tactile Fabrics Enabled by Liquid Metal Core–Sheath Yarns for High-Fidelity Electronic Skins
abstract: Piezoresistive tactile fabrics for wearable electronics are fundamentally limited by the conflicting needs for high-pressure sensitivity and stable signal transmission, as conventional yarns can suffer from severe inter-pixel crosstalk and strain-induced signal drift. To address this, we present a strain-tolerant tactile fabric using a core–sheath yarn architecture that spatially decouples sensing and conduction. The core, fabricated from silver nanoparticle-decorated styrene butadiene styrene (SBS) yarns and eutectic gallium–indium (EGaIn), provides high electromechanical stability at large strains for robust signal transmission. Simultaneously, a carbon nanotube/polyurethane sheath ensures high piezoresistive sensitivity for precise pressure detection. Weaving these yarns into an 8 × 8 array effectively suppresses tensile and pressure-induced crosstalk (< 5% error) under 20% strain or concurrent multi-point pressing (up to 665 kPa). Integrated into a smart glove with deep learning, the system demonstrates a 99.2% accuracy in recognizing object shapes, representing a dramatic enhancement over the 32.2% accuracy of counterparts composed of homogeneous piezoresistive yarns without core–sheath architecture. This scalable strategy overcomes intrinsic trade-offs in stretchable sensing, advancing high-fidelity electronic skins for human–machine interaction, robotics, and telemedicine.

title: Hierarchical Cellulose–COF Composite Membranes with Dual-Sieving Channels for High-Flux and High-Selectivity Separation
abstract: Covalent organic framework (COF) membranes, with their programmable pore structures and tunable chemical environments, hold great promise for water purification and pollutant separation. However, simultaneously achieving high permeability and selectivity remains a key challenge. Inspired by the biomineralization mechanism of diatom cell walls, we constructed a bioinspired hierarchical nanofiltration membrane by integrating electrospun cellulose nanofibers with in situ grown COF layers (ECNF/COF membrane). The membrane features multiscale transport channels comprising neck-bridged microsphere junctions, intraparticle tortuous pathways, and intrinsic COF nanopores, enabling efficient and selective molecular transport. Thiol–ene click functionalization with sulfonic acid groups produced the ECNF/SCOF membrane and simultaneously regulated wettability (water contact angle from 150.4° to 2.7°), surface charge (zeta potential from −1.5 to −21.8 mV), and pore size (from 2.8 to 1.4 nm). The ECNF/COF and ECNF/SCOF membranes exhibited excellent separation efficiencies (> 99%) for W/O and O/W emulsions, respectively. In mixed dye/salt systems, the ECNF/SCOF membrane achieved over 99% dye rejection while maintaining high salt permeability (salt rejection below 10%). Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed a synergistic “size-sieving plus electrostatic-barrier” mechanism, clarifying the interplay between structure and surface chemistry. This work proposes a programmable, multiscale structure–interface co-regulation strategy that offers new insights into high-performance purification in complex liquid pollution systems. title: Dynamic Interfacial Fusion Enables Scalable Production of Mechanically Robust Self‐Adhesive Cellulose Paper
abstract: Cellulose paper is a promising sustainable alternative to replace plastic films, but its mechanical weakness limits practical applications. While strategies, such as molecular alignment and composite reinforcement, can enhance strength, their complex and costly processing hinders scalable production. We present a dynamic interfacial fusion strategy that dramatically enhances the mechanical strength of commercial nanofibril and microfibril cellulose papers, achieving universal applicability across diverse raw material sources. We demonstrate that metastable swelling of cellulose molecules triggers spontaneous interfacial fused entanglement, unlocking an approximately 73.8% enhancement of strength. The tensile strength of fused cellulose paper is up to 203.4 MPa, surpassing most conventional plastic films. This simple swelling-fusion process enables large-scale production of high-strength papers with lengths exceeding 100 m and is compatible with diverse paper sources, including bamboo, cotton, wood pulp, and even commercial papers (A4 paper and cellophane). Furthermore, the intermolecular fusion imparts self-adhesion properties to the cellulose papers without requiring chemical adhesives, offering a green pathway to fabricate robust three-dimensional assemblies. This universal fusion strategy bridges the gap between sustainable cellulose materials and industrial-scale production, offering a viable plastic alternative for applications in daily packaging, electronics, and biomedical components.
